newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish steel shares rise after results.
newsitem.headline: Swedish steel shares rise after results.

text.p: Swedish-British steel company Avesta Sheffield and Sweden's SSAB both rose on Friday after posting 1996 results, but analysts said gains in Avesta Sheffield were more difficult to justify.
"Fundamentals look entirely different for the two companies," said Anders Trapp, Enskilda analyst.
SSAB and Avesta Sheffield on Thursday reported falling earnings because of a weak market and lower steel prices.
In late trade Friday SSAB was five crowns higher at 123.5 after gaining 3.5 crowns on Thursday and Avesta Sheffield rose 1.5 crowns to 77.5 after gaining 1.5 crowns a day earlier.
Carbon steel maker SSAB showed a 45 percent drop in 1996 profit after financial items to 2.09 billion crowns.

Stainless steel manufacturer Avesta Sheffield plunged into the red in the first nine months of its fiscal year 1996/1997, reporting a pretax loss of 136 million crowns, compared with a pretax profit of 3.15 billion.
"I don't understand why Avesta is doing so well. Price developments don't look good while at the same time they have had problems with production," Swedbank analyst Mats Larsson told Reuters.
Some said the rise in the Avesta Sheffield price could be fuelled by a rumour that the group's British owner would bid for the Swedish half of the company.
This was more likely when the share price was not especially high, analysts said.
"British Steel is always waiting in the wings," one analyst said.
Many of Avesta Sheffield's costs were one-off expenses and Avesta Sheffield did say it expected higher prices as of April following some producers annnouncing price hikes of seven to eight percent.
Analysts say the SSAB result was better than expected.
"SSABAS is an amazingly well-managed company, but overcapitalised," one analyst said, but added it was a disappointment that the company did not increase its dividend from four crowns a share.
The company's large cash flows may become a problem, another analyst said.
"Gradually they will find it difficult to get a good return on their capital," one analyst said.
